newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia economic growth forecast lowered.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia economic growth forecast lowered.

text.p: Economists have lowered their forecast for Malaysia's economic growth this year and in 1998 due to slower-than-expected export growth and high interest rates, a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.
In the poll, 12 research houses in Malaysia and Singapore forecast an average 7.9 percent gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1997 against the 8.0 percent they projected at the end of last year.
The government has forecast a growth of 7.8-8.2 percent after reporting rise of 8.2 percent in 1996.
The economists forecast the 1998 GDP growth at an average 7.4 percent.

The houses polled were Crosby Research, J.M. Sassoon & Co, Jupiter Securities, Kleinwort Benson, Merrill Lynch, MMS International, Natwest Markets, OSK Research, Phileo Allied Securities, TA Securities, UBS Securities and Vickers Ballas.
Their forecasts for the current year ranged between 7.5 and 8.2 percent and for 1998 between 5.4 and 8.0 percent.
Economists said they had also mostly revised downward their growth projections after taking into account the recent currency turmoil.
The Malaysian ringgit has fallen more than 11 percent against the dollar to a 42-month low of 2.7930 on Tuesday over the past month due to heavy selling by offshore funds.
The ringgit was around 2.7700 to a dollar at 0700 GMT.

"Most people are knocking down their numbers after recent developments," said Kevin Chew, economist at Caspian Securities. "The ringgit is weakening and the period of high interest rates is longer than what we have anticipated. This will curb domestic demand."
Heavy intervention by the central Bank Negara Malaysia in June to defend the ringgit mopped up large funds from the banking system, pushing interbank rates sharply higher.
Slower exports and foreign investment had also prompted economists to lower their forecast.
Malaysian exports in the first six months of this year rose by only 1.9 percent, to 98.4 billion ringgit against the same period of 1996.
The slower export growth in part contributed to Malaysia's unexpectedly large trade deficit of 2.8 billion ringgit for June.
Malaysia's approvals of foreign investment slumped to 5.41 billion ringgit in the first half of this year, against 17.06 billion ringgit for the whole of 1996, government figures showed.
